items.title: Researcher demonstrates data exfiltration from Claude AI assistant using web browsing capabilities to leak personal information [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: I tricked Claude into leaking your deepest, darkest secrets
items.summary:
A researcher explored security vulnerabilities in the Claude AI assistant's memory system and demonstrated how it could be tricked into leaking sensitive personal information such as full name, employer, and security question answers. The experiment exploited Claude's web browsing tools, particularly the web_fetch feature, to navigate a controlled website and exfiltrate data through URL requests without detection.

The researcher found that Claude's memory system stores detailed user profiles, which could be used maliciously if accessed improperly. Although Anthropic implemented safeguards restricting web_fetch to specific URL criteria, the researcher bypassed these by creating a navigable web directory that Claude could follow autonomously. This approach allowed the extraction of private data despite the AI's sandboxing and security measures.

The findings highlight potential risks in AI assistants that accumulate extensive personal data and use web browsing tools, emphasizing the need for stronger security controls to prevent unauthorized data leakage or exploitation.

items.title: Mindgard reports unpatched Cursor IDE vulnerability allowing automatic execution of malicious git.exe in project roots, persisting over six months despite multiple disclosures [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Cursor 0day: When Full Disclosure Becomes the Only Protection Left
items.summary:
Mindgard disclosed a critical vulnerability in the Cursor AI-assisted development environment that allows arbitrary code execution when opening a project containing a malicious git.exe in the repository root on Windows. This issue requires no user interaction and has remained unpatched for over six months despite repeated reports and engagement attempts with Cursor's security team. Cursor, used by millions of developers and thousands of companies, continues to ship new versions without addressing the flaw.

The vulnerability was first reported in December 2025 and confirmed by HackerOne, but Cursor's response has been minimal, with the bug bounty report initially closed as out of scope and subsequent follow-ups ignored. Mindgard recommends temporary mitigations such as using AppLocker policies on managed Windows systems or opening untrusted repositories in isolated environments until a fix is released. The case raises concerns about Cursor's security processes and transparency with affected users.

items.title: LeMario: Training a JEPA World Model on Super Mario Bros to predict game dynamics and plan reward-free actions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LeMario: Training a JEPA World Model on Super Mario Bros
items.summary:
LeMario is a project that implements a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) trained on Super Mario Bros gameplay frames and actions to learn world dynamics without rewards. The model encodes game frames and actions into latent representations and uses a transformer-based predictor with adaptive normalization to forecast future states, aiming to enable reward-free planning in the game.

The model was trained on over 700,000 frames from 280 episodes across 32 levels and demonstrated the ability to generalize to unseen episodes and predict several steps ahead better than baselines. However, while it could move Mario toward nearby image goals, it struggled with longer-range planning and navigating major obstacles, indicating it learned to predict game states but not necessarily how to progress through the levels. The project includes a detailed technical walkthrough and analysis of the model's architecture, training process, and limitations.

items.title: OpenAI employees donate over $215,000 to Guardrails Alliance super PAC opposing AI industry group led by OpenAI president Greg Brockman [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI Staffers Are Funding a Rival Super PAC to Take on Their Boss
items.summary:
Several current and former OpenAI employees have contributed more than $215,000 to Guardrails Alliance, a super PAC advocating for stricter AI regulations and opposing Leading the Future, a pro-AI industry group supported by OpenAI president Greg Brockman. Guardrails Alliance launched with $5 million in funding and aims to raise $15 million this election cycle to counterbalance the $100 million backing Leading the Future has received from tech leaders.

The donations from OpenAI staff highlight internal tensions over the company's political influence and AI policy direction, as some employees express concern about Brockman's involvement with Leading the Future. OpenAI has stated that Brockman's political activities are personal and not representative of the company, while employees are free to engage politically on their own. Guardrails Alliance cofounder Shaunna Thomas emphasized that their strategy relies on public opinion rather than matching the opposition's financial resources dollar-for-dollar.

items.title: ASML raises 2026 sales forecast to €43-45 billion after Q2 beats guidance with €9.3 billion revenue, citing strong AI-driven chip demand [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: What Do ASML's Q2 2026 Results Tell Us About the AI Boom?
items.summary:
ASML reported Q2 2026 net sales of €9.3 billion and net income of €2.9 billion, exceeding its guidance and prompting the company to raise its full-year sales forecast to €43-45 billion from €36-40 billion. CEO Christophe Fouquet attributed the strong first-half order intake to AI-related investments driving demand for advanced logic and memory chips, leading ASML to plan a 30% increase in EUV system capacity for 2027 and consider further expansion in 2028.

China accounted for roughly 20% of ASML's sales despite the MATCH Act restrictions on DUV exports, with demand focused on logic chips for domestic customers. The company noted that the legislation has not yet impacted its order book, but the compliance window closing in late September could affect future sales. ASML's outlook aligns with strong performance from key customers like TSMC and SK Hynix, indicating sustained growth across the AI chip supply chain.

This achievement marks Level 1 recursive self-improvement, where the system improves itself more efficiently than human researchers under a fixed compute budget.

The conclusion emphasizes choosing formats that balance human reviewability, tool compatibility, and efficient AI consumption rather than just minimizing token count.

items.summary:
Way to go, Demis Hassabis! The Google DeepMind co-founder and CEO won plaudits from much of the AI industry—including rivals OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Block co-founder Jack Dorsey and investors Ashton Kutcher and Chamath Palihapitiya—for proposing the creation of a new AI standards group funded by industry but working with government. 

Hassabis’ idea is that this new group could review frontier AI models to ensure they don’t pose a danger in areas such as cybersecurity and biological threats or in any other way (more here). Industry peers generally called the proposal “thoughtful,” although Nadella labeled it “important” and Palihapitiya described it as “well reasoned.” (Kutcher settled for “agreed.”) Unfortunately, those accolades won’t get us far.

items.originalTitle: Prepare for Customer Calls with Google Gemini
items.summary:
Pitching a new customer for the first time can be intimidating.

Especially if most of your conversations are with existing clients and warm leads, it is often difficult to know where to start with a new customer. The prospect may know little to nothing about your product or service offering, and it is easy to fall into the trap of over-explaining, racing through as much information as possible out of fear of leaving something out.

Gemini can help you get beyond the blank page and the blinking cursor. By providing Gemini with specific information about your product and the prospect’s needs, you can generate first drafts of custom call scripts and elevator pitches in record time—and then go back and forth in a natural-language chat until you feel fully prepared for your pitch meeting.

Step 1: Generate a Custom Script

Don’t let perfectionism keep you from getting started. Instead, quickly gather the information that is relevant to your upcoming call and upload it to Gemini. This might include product one-pagers, offer sheets, pricing pages, and any input forms or other information that the prospect has already provided. More is usually better, but Gemini can get started with whatever you have at your fingertips.

Next, type a prompt asking Gemini to draft a call script. Your prompt doesn’t need to be more than a few sentences, but it should be as detailed as possible to make sure Gemini understands what you’re looking for. Here’s an example:

Draft a customized script for me to follow during my sales call with a prospect. The call will happen over a video call and is set to last 30 minutes. Make sure to add the following in the script: how [company products/solutions] can help address potential customer’s pain points, how [company]’s delivery system guarantees seamless and timely delivery, competitive pricing and volume-discount table, and space for a customer reference in the [customer’s industry] industry.

Step 2: Refine Your Pitch

Remember that Gemini’s response is a starting point, not a finished product. You may find that your own thinking becomes sharper the moment you have a draft that you can react to.

When Gemini produces an insightful angle or clever transition, these might spark your imagination, inspiring you to build on what’s already there. Or, if a section feels out-of-place or doesn’t align with your own voice, you may find yourself pushing back with better ideas. Either way, having a “thought partner” can be invaluable as you revise the initial draft into a polished pitch.

items.originalTitle: Evaluating Models is Getting Even Harder
items.summary:
As AI gets more advanced, researchers are increasingly telling me that it’s also getting harder to evaluate how good AI actually is at various tasks. 

Most obviously, as AI improves, it quickly saturates all the benchmarks we have today and researchers have to rush to come up with even harder evaluations that the models won’t immediately ace.

There are more subtle reasons as well. Researchers at the International Conference on Machine Learning said last week that today’s models have gotten so good, they can work on a task for hours or days. That’s great, but it also means evaluating their performance can take hours or days as well.

We’re quickly approaching a point where models can “work for weeks or indefinitely,” OpenAI researcher Noam Brown said during an ICML panel last week. (You can imagine that a model would want to work for that long in cases like drug discovery, where a model might spend weeks running experiments and analyzing the results of those experiments.) That means evaluating a model could eventually take longer than training that model in the first place, Brown said. Not only is that difficult to do practically, but it could also slow down the process of model development.

Suddenly everyone wants to hand the government a piece of AI. Sam Altman has discussed giving up a stake in OpenAI. Washington already owns 10% of Intel and has said it will take a cut of Nvidia’s China chip revenue. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) wants every major AI lab to put half of its stock into a new sovereign wealth fund.

In soccer terms, these are shots on goal, but nobody is scoring.

Every one of these proposals ends in the same place: equity parked with the government. The Treasury gets richer, or a fund gets set up. Not one of them says what happens to an actual citizen—how a person earns a stake, holds it or ever sees a dollar from it. This is a big problem that the tech giants haven’t solved.

Luckily, big ideas can come from small towns, so let me take you to one.
